intro.en: Bedside vocabulary for describing paediatric rashes and bleeding spots by appearance and size.

title.en: Naming skin lesions by look and size

items.summary: Standard bedside words for paediatric eruptions, sorting flat patches, raised bumps, fluid filled blisters, pus filled spots and bleeding lesions by feel and diameter.

blocks.title: Rash words for skin versus lining membranes
bullets: Exanthem means a visible eruption spread over the outer skin.
Enanthem means a similar eruption over a moist lining membrane.

blocks.title: Lesion chart by feel and measured size

head: Term
What the examiner sees and feels
rows: Level patch of altered colour or texture that cannot be felt.
Small firm raised bump smaller than 0.5 cm across.
Bigger firm raised lump larger than 0.5 cm across.
Small blister holding clear fluid, under 0.5 cm across.
Large fluid filled blister wider than 0.5 cm.
Raised lesion with yellow pus plainly visible inside the skin.
Pinpoint bleeding spots in skin under 2 mm wide.
Broad bruise like bleed wider than 10 mm.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The book separates raised solid lesions and blisters at a 0.5 cm diameter cutoff.
Bleeding lesions step up in the same way: under 2 mm, then 2-10 mm, then above 10 mm.

viva.q: How do you separate a papule from a nodule, and a vesicle from bullae?
viva.a: By a 0.5 cm diameter cutoff. Papules and vesicles lie below it, nodules and bullae above; vesicles and bullae contain fluid while papules and nodules are solid.

viva.q: What is the difference between an exanthem and an enanthem?
viva.a: An exanthem erupts on the outer skin, while an enanthem erupts on a moist lining membrane such as inside the mouth.

viva.q: How do petechiae, purpura and ecchymosis differ?
viva.a: All are skin bleeds graded by width: petechiae under 2 mm, purpura 2-10 mm, and ecchymosis above 10 mm.
